# Moving from Cloud Functions to a ¥4,300 server: ¥3,700 a day, Yahoo! failing in the EEA, and five traps

  日本語版 (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/vps-migration/)

Written by Koshin (https://koshinstudio.com/en/about/#operator) (web engineer and app engineer) · published 2026-10-17
Development log of the Toreca Dash app / August 2026

  The back end of my iPhone app Toreca Dash originally ran on Google Cloud Functions (billed per function for the time it runs). When the free trial ended on 16 August 2026, from 17 August it cost about ¥3,700 a day (about ¥106,000 a month).

  This article records how I moved that code almost unchanged to a server (VPS) at about ¥4,300 a month: what I decided, what I corrected later, and the traps.

  Numbers come from my work log of 20 August 2026. I do not include server addresses or connection details.

## Why move: waiting time was billed too

  About 97% of the Cloud Functions bill was CPU time (vCPU seconds). But nearly all of my functions just wait for scraping targets and AI replies, and that waiting was billed in full.

  On a flat-rate server that structural waste disappears.

  I also considered Cloudflare Workers. The Firestore admin SDK does not run there and hundreds of places would need rewriting to another API, so I dropped it. On a VPS the current code runs as is.

## What I chose, and where I first got it wrong

    Item | Details

      Provider | Hetzner Cloud

      Spec | 2 vCPU, 4 GB memory, 80 GB SSD

      Location | Singapore

      Price | €26.99 a month (about ¥4,300)

  I first built it in Helsinki (€5.99 a month). Then I rebuilt it.

  The reason: Yahoo! Shopping’s API blocks access from the EEA and the UK. Calling it from Helsinki returned not the API response but a notice page, “For customers in the European Economic Area and the UK”, with HTTP 403. All 15 genres failed. It is a legal geo-block, not bot detection, so retrying never helps. From Singapore it returns HTTP 200 normally.

  I deleted the Helsinki server; it had cost €0.02 (about ¥3).

  Hetzner’s pricing gives a €7 a month discount only in three European locations. The cheapest line (CX) is sold only in Europe. So “cheap location = EEA = Yahoo! dies”. Do not go back to Europe for the price.

  Singapore also helped by being closer to Japanese sites: the Pokémon card new-arrival check went from 52.7 seconds to 15.8 seconds (3.3× faster).

## Run the code unchanged: intercept require

  I wrote a runner (runner.js). The original code (index.js) is not changed at all.

  Instead of copying 132 schedules by hand, I intercept require and replace firebase-functions with my own, making the calls that register schedules just add to a list. Then I load the original code, and all definitions are collected automatically. The counts collected:

  132 scheduled jobs / 256 HTTP endpoints / 9 Firestore triggers
  Not copying by hand was right. One schedule is written as the template string `every ${X_CHECK_INTERVAL_MINUTES} minutes`. Copying by eye would have got it wrong. I matched all 132 mechanically and confirmed they agree.

  The 9 Firestore triggers (functions that fire when data changes) do not fire on the VPS. I left them on Cloud Functions (they are event-driven and cost almost nothing). The 256 HTTP endpoints stay there too, because the app and admin page call them.

## Five traps I hit in the move

### 1. There were 15 secrets, not 5

  My earlier notes said “5 secrets”. Counting every environment variable in the code gave 15. The missing 10 included Rakuten, Google Maps, Yahoo!, X authentication, the billing integration, a membership-site session and a debug secret.

  A missed secret does not raise an error; it quietly returns 0 results. Extract the variable names from the code mechanically and count them.

### 2. A secret value contained newlines

  The membership-site session secret is in a “one line per site” format, so the value itself contains newlines. Written naively into an env file, line two onwards becomes separate variables and 3 of 4 sites quietly die. I made the env-file reader understand escaped newlines (\n).

### 3. A write-blocked rehearsal looped forever

  Rakuten’s and Yahoo!’s APIs need a spacing between calls (rate limiting). The code writes “last call time” to Firestore and waits until it advances. In a rehearsal where all writes were swallowed, the time never advanced and the loop never ended. (Cloud Functions was also updating it every 1.5 seconds, so “someone else updated it, wait again” repeated forever. A Rakuten Ichiba job not returning for over 15 minutes revealed it.) In rehearsal I let just that rate-limit record through.

### 4. “Writes on, notifications off” silently deletes notifications

  The job that sends notifications in batches deletes the pending list once it counts them as sent. Stubbing only the sending while allowing writes would delete without sending, losing notifications. So during the rehearsal stage I did not register seven notification-related schedules on the VPS. They are removed from the skip list only when notifications are turned on.

### 5. A new exit IP quietly stops one scraper

  A supermarket site was fetched with a plain request and had no fallback. From Japan it was 200, from Singapore 403. I compared all 75 hosts from both Japan and Singapore: 6 are “visible from Japan, not from Singapore”; 5 of those already went through the scraping service or had a fallback and were fine. Only one broke. “403 from Singapore” alone is not proof of breakage. Check whether it goes through the scraping service.

## The order of the move: not to send notifications twice

- Stage 1: read only (no writes, no notifications) and compare fetch counts with Cloud Functions.

- Stage 2: write, but leave notifications to Cloud Functions.

- Stage 3: delete only the 132 scheduled functions from Cloud Functions.

- Stage 4: turn notifications on in the VPS.

  Always keep exactly one side sending notifications. If both send at once, users get the same notification twice.

## What I learned

> A service billed by time does not suit code that mostly waits.

- Look at the billing unit. If waiting is billed, scraping and AI calls are expensive.

- Hosting has legal limits. The cheap place may be a place you cannot use.

- Look for a way to move without rewriting. Interception and mechanical matching avoided hand-copy errors.

- Count settings by machine. 15, not 5.

- Move in stages to avoid duplicate notifications.

  This is the English version of the original Japanese article (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/vps-migration/).

  More in English

- All English pages (https://koshinstudio.com/en/)

- Toreca Dash (https://koshinstudio.com/en/works/torecadash/)

# I opened the links of displayed articles and compared them: about 60 mistakes, and three mistakes in my own first check

  日本語版 (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/destination-check/)

Written by Koshin (https://koshinstudio.com/en/about/#operator) (web engineer and app engineer) · published 2026-10-17
Development log of the Toreca Dash app / September 2026

  The articles in my app Toreca Dash link to store and shopping-site pages. Even if an article’s title and price are right, if the linked page is closed or about a different product, it is no use to the user.

  On the night of 15 September 2026, asked to “check the destination content too”, I actually opened the links of displayed articles and compared the content with the article: product, store, whether open, sale type, deadline and price. About 60 mistakes turned up.

  Numbers come from my work log of 15 September 2026. The check itself made no writes; I fixed the findings separately.

## How I checked

- X posts (361): 0 deleted. The text had been compared in earlier checks.

- Non-X (703, excluding Yahoo!): I read the destination directly or via the scraping service (with a Japanese IP) and judged with an AI. Amazon always goes through the scraping service.

  My first version of the check got three things wrong:

- I opened Amazon from Singapore. Prices showed in Singapore dollars and I saw another seller, and judged that “wrong”.

- I read Rakuten as garbled text. I had not detected the character encoding (EUC-JP).

- I opened 501 Yahoo! pages six at a time. The production IP was refused with HTTP 489 (see another article (https://koshinstudio.com/en/notes/self-inflicted/)). I stopped partway through Yahoo!.

  If the checking tool is wrong, the count of “mistakes” inflates. I fixed encoding detection, opening Amazon from Japan, and judging only by stock of “this exact item”, then reran.

## Mistakes found (about 60)

    What | Count | Fix

      Amazon “invitation request” shown as pre-order or first-come | 10 | Make it a lottery

      Amazon “pre-order” shown as first-come | 7 | Make it a reservation

      Rakuten Books “pre-orders open” shown as first-come | 3 | Make it a reservation

      Shops closed temporarily (Yahoo!) | 6 | Hide

      Sold out or closed but still displayed | many | Hide

      Link goes to a different store or an ended lottery | 3 | Go back to the store’s X post

      Link goes to a different product | 2 | Hide

      Price mismatch | about 10 | Correct

      Empty store name | 1 | Fill in

  The most frequent was the wrong sale type. On Amazon there are “invitation requests”, neither first-come nor pre-order. Treating one as first-come means users cannot buy however fast they are. The earlier code only marked the invitation and did not correct the sale type.

  Some sold-out pages did not match my sold-out wording. A Yahoo! sold-out page says “out of stock” on screen, but matched none of the keywords. So I now judge by the stock data embedded in the page for that item ("stock":{"isAvailable":false). The data is more reliable than the wording on screen.

## “Opening the application link goes to the site’s top page”

  Found in another check the same day. The QR code on a store’s lottery image pointed to a URL that, actually opened, redirects to the site’s top page, not an application page.

  I added a check to the single gate that adopts application links. It opens the URL, and if the original URL has a path other than the top but the destination path is empty (or a file name that looks like a top page), it does not adopt it. If it cannot be read (403, timeout), it still adopts, since many stores use bot protection and unreadable is not a sign of badness. The same URL is held for 6 hours.

## What I did not fix, and could not fix

  It matters that I did not count everything found as a “mistake”. There are cases I checked and did not fix.

- Rakuten Ichiba “sold out”: the page data said in stock (a setting hides stock counts). The AI misread it.

- Amazon “See all buying options”: other sellers exist, so it is not necessarily sold out.

- Amazon English titles: auto-translated names; the product was right.

- 85 pages I could not read: Rakuten Ichiba (via ad links), membership sites, LINE, Google Forms and so on.

  I keep results in three groups with reasons: fixed, not fixed, could not read. “Not fixed” needs a reason too.

## What I learned

> Even if title and price match, you cannot know until you open the link.

- Actually open the link. Looking only at the article cannot show that the destination is closed.

- Check the checking tool first. Country, encoding, parallelism: a wrong tool inflates “mistakes”.

- Embedded data beats screen wording. Judge sold-out by stock data, not text.

- Do not make everything found a “mistake”. Keep reasons for what you do not fix.

- Do not treat “could not read” as bad. Bot protection makes unreadable normal.

  This is the English version of the original Japanese article (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/destination-check/).

  More in English

- All English pages (https://koshinstudio.com/en/)

- Toreca Dash (https://koshinstudio.com/en/works/torecadash/)

# Four things from a full sweep of 61 audits: 51 jobs clumped at 4 a.m., a lock that expired in 55 seconds, and a price-filling idea I decided not to add

  日本語版 (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/audit-sweep-61/)

Written by Koshin (https://koshinstudio.com/en/about/#operator) (web engineer and app engineer) · published 2026-10-17
Development log of the Toreca Dash app / September 2026

  My app Toreca Dash has 61 audits that find anomalies. In the early hours of 8 September 2026 I ran them all and checked every item that was not 0 against real data, one by one.

  This article is four stories from that work. Three are things I fixed; one is a story where I measured, and deliberately did not add it.

  Numbers come from my work log of the evening of 7 to the morning of 8 September 2026.

## 1. 51 once-a-day jobs were clumped at 4 and 5 a.m.

  At 04:53 the measurements were:

- The 14 concurrency slots were full, 8 waiting.

- 6 jobs timed out at the 540-second limit.

- The “instant sell-out monitor” and the “Amazon fastest lane” I wanted to protect were skipped 9 times each per hour.

  The cause was clumping in time. Counting once-a-day jobs: 27 at 4 o’clock and 24 at 5; at 1 o’clock and from 10 to 21, 0.

  The fix was not to edit times one by one, which would not apply to jobs added later. I fixed the mechanism that spreads start times. The spread was a flat 270 seconds; for jobs with an interval of 6 hours or more it now spreads up to 1,800 seconds (30 minutes). 27 jobs over 30 minutes is about one per 67 seconds, so 3 to 5 run at once.

  I kept it to 30 minutes so it does not spill into the next hour’s slot and break time-based order like “check at 2, fill at 3”.

## 2. A patrol meant to be “every minute” took 181 to 480 seconds per run

  The Rakuten Ichiba patrol was meant to run every minute. Measured, one run took 181 to 480 seconds. The harm was threefold:

- It occupied a concurrency slot almost all the time.

- It timed out at the 480-second limit (4 times in 2 hours) and the results were thrown away.

- It held the Rakuten API allowance (one call per 1.5 seconds, shared by all jobs) the whole time, cutting the share of the instant sell-out monitor.

  The effective interval was 3.5 to 6 minutes. And after a timeout it restarts from the same first genre every time, so later genres never get a turn.

  I switched it to the five-genres-at-a-time rotation proven on Rakuten Books.

     | Before | After

      One run | 181–480 s | 50–83 s

      Timeouts | 4 per 2 hours | 0

      Interval per genre | 3.5–6 min | 3 min

  I found one more thing. The lock that means “if the previous run is still going, do not start” (preventing double runs) expired after only 55 seconds. For jobs with a 480-second limit and 181–480 s real runs, a run that slipped past the runner’s skip (a manual run, a catch-up right after restart) could run twice at once, doubling Rakuten API use and hitting first-come monitoring. I set both to 480,000 ms. A lock’s expiry should be at least the job’s timeout.

## 3. Stop counting anomalies you cannot fix

  If you keep counting things that cannot be fixed, real anomalies get buried. I revisited three.

- “Lottery with no deadline: 77” became 0. Scanning the text of all 89 real cases, only 5 contained a date-like value, and those were not application deadlines (“lottery results 9/5”, “pick up by 9/13”). The store simply did not write one, and nothing can be done. Now only items that have both deadline wording and a date in the text count as anomalies.

- “3 stopped scrapers” became 0. What was counted were state records with no run time, not jobs. The main code excludes them, only the audit did not.

- One store’s “0 items for 173 hours” was normal. Fetching its three categories worked (16 and 6 items), and all were “point-exchange only” (0 yen). There was just no lottery or pre-order at the time.

  But “0 items” has two meanings: (a) no product matches (normal), (b) the page layout changed and nothing can be read (broken). If you cannot tell them apart, real breakage is buried (the previous day’s Pokémon Center (https://koshinstudio.com/en/notes/blocked-page/) was exactly this). So I now put the number scanned into the completion message.

## 4. A case I measured and deliberately did not add

  397 products had unknown official prices, which stops first-come notifications. The filling job had, measured, zero results.

  Official price unset: 397
Has a price at a regular store: 51
Two or more stores agree: 0
  The “two or more stores agree” condition had effectively never been satisfied. Accepting one store would fill 51. All were kinds with no catalogue price (imported Magic cards and so on).

  I still did not add it. Regular stores discount. If I record a discounted price as the official price, the price check’s ceiling (official price × 1.08 plus margin) becomes lower than the real price and legitimate listings are removed as resale. At 10% off, the real price is 1.11× and exceeds the ceiling. And over-deletion draws no complaints, so I would not notice.

  I wrote down what to do first if I add it:

- Compare the 51 prices by eye with official sites and the manufacturer’s suggested price (confirm whether they are discounted; do not guess a factor).

- Mark single-store-based prices and add margin to the ceiling only for that mark.

- After adding, count hidden articles before and after.

## What I learned

> Clumping is invisible until counted. Record the decision not to add, too.

- Count clumping in time. 27 at 4 o’clock, 0 from 10 to 21.

- Jobs hold something you cannot see. A lock’s expiry should be at least the timeout.

- Do not count anomalies you cannot fix. If the number does not fit, doubt how you count.

- Distinguish what “0 items” means. Show the number scanned.

- If you decide not to add something, keep the reason and the conditions. Even when measurement shows a gain, if it risks over-deleting, I do not add it.

  This is the English version of the original Japanese article (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/audit-sweep-61/).

- Toreca Dash (https://koshinstudio.com/en/works/torecadash/)

# Comparing with other sites to count gaps: the first “23% coverage” was a measuring mistake and the truth was 49%

  日本語版 (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/coverage-check/)

Written by Koshin (https://koshinstudio.com/en/about/#operator) (web engineer and app engineer) · published 2026-10-17
Development log of the Toreca Dash app / August 2026

  One goal of my app Toreca Dash is to show lottery information without leaving anything out. The best way to find gaps is to compare with other sites that publish the same information and count “what they have and I do not”.

  I did this in the early hours of 29 August 2026. The first number was “23% coverage”. But that was a mistake in how I measured. This article records the five problems found as the number moved from 23% to 49% and then 90%.

  Numbers come from my work log of 29 August 2026. I do not name other sites.

## First, I surveyed every competitor

  The request was: “remove every article competitors publish that this app does not”. First I surveyed every possible competitor. Whether I could import from each was decided by reading the robots.txt (the request to machines) and the terms of use in full.

    What I found | Count | Handling

      Sites I already imported from | 3 | Unchanged

      Site newly added this time (Site A) | 1 | Per-case entries, with application links

      Sites whose terms have no prohibition and can be imported | 2 | Compared by hand this time

      Explainer-style sites with no per-store list | several | Skipped: almost no difference

      Sites whose robots.txt and terms prohibit automated fetching | 2 | Not imported. Not allowed as application links either

      A site whose domain no longer exists | 1 | Removed from the list

  One site states the prohibition in Japanese at the very top of its robots.txt. That a machine can fetch it does not mean it should.

## The comparison site was finer-grained than mine

  The site I added (Site A) lists “store × product × deadline × application link”, 90 entries on a single page. My sources were per-article, A is per-case, and its application links are the external forms themselves (Google Forms, LivePocket, Lottery Rotobox, the store’s official X). It was a good counterpart both for counting and for filling gaps.

## Problem 1: a different way of writing a product name counted as “missed”

  The first number was 23% coverage. Reason one was how product names are written.

  Them  30th CELEBRATION BOX
Mine  Expansion Pack "30th CELEBRATION"
  Neither contains the other, so naive “contains” never matches. 60 entries were counted as missed because of this.

  But “same if contained” is not the answer. The name “30th CELEBRATION” is contained in “30th CELEBRATION Premium Deck Set”. That errs in the direction of counting a different product as “covered”, hiding holes.

  The fix: drop set-type words (expansion pack, high-class pack) and quantity words (BOX, n-piece set, n types), then link to a catalogue product ID. The order: exact match, then the longest catalogue name contained in their name, then the reverse only when there is exactly one.

## Problem 2: an expired article counted as “covered”

  Reason two was 5 entries. An article with a 29 July deadline at one store was paired with their 30 August case and reported as “article exists but hidden”. It was a different, earlier lottery. After these two fixes the true number was 49%.

## Problem 3: articles made to fill gaps landed on the wrong product

  Gaps are filled by creating articles. But I passed their product name to an AI as is. The AI linked “30th CELEBRATION BOX” to “30th CELEBRATION FUTURISTIC BOX”, priced at ¥27,500. 10 articles ended up on the wrong product.

  The counting side had already narrowed to one catalogue product. The right fix was to give the creating side my catalogue name: one judgement for counting and creating.

  While repairing, I made another mistake. I wrote product IDs truncated to the first 10 characters and created 10 articles with nonexistent IDs. My check printed IDs with slice(0, 10) to read them, and I used those short values directly. I fixed it at once, and the rule is now: never use an ID shortened for display in processing.

## Problem 4: application links other than t.co were always discarded

  The step that attaches application links to aggregator-derived articles passed each store’s URL through a link-expanding function. That function only looks at t.co (X’s short URL), because links in X posts are always shortened. Other sources hold application URLs in plain form. Through it, they gave 0 results every time and fell back to web search.

  Of 32 articles made from Site A, 17 pointed to the source site’s page rather than the application form. Sending users to the source site was something I had decided to prohibit.

  The fix: use plain, unshortened URLs as candidates directly (the usual check still decides adoption). For articles already made, I added a step that rewrites the application link on every comparison, and rewrote 16.

## Problem 5: articles hidden for “no deadline” had no way back

  A job hid aggregator-derived articles whose deadline was unknown. It only hid; even if the deadline became known later, it stayed hidden forever. It is the same shape as an alert that keeps ringing after the fix. For cases where the other site gives a deadline, I now set it and restore the article (articles hidden for other reasons are not restored). Two were restored.

  I also fixed how deadline times are handled. The parsed date was returned as a “Japan-time shifted” value and, saved as is, would have been a deadline 9 hours off. 23:59 Japan time is 14:59 UTC; I now return the real time.

## Result

     | Count

      Open cases Site A lists | 86

      Shown in my app | 77 (90% coverage)

      Missing from the feed | 0

      Article exists but hidden | 2

      Cannot create because they do not identify the product | 7

  This work created 32 articles, rewrote 16 application links and restored 2 with deadlines.

  The remaining 9 all have known reasons:

- One store’s premium deck set is deliberately excluded, because its application page says only “for one box of the expansion pack”. Here the other side is wrong.

- Seven “Starter Set ex, 3 types” entries: the other side does not say which 3 types either. Guessing three articles would put articles about other products side by side, so I do not create them.

- The last is one article hidden for not being seen recently. It may also need a “way back” and stays on my to-do list.

## What I learned

> A flaw in the counting tool does not make the number look bad; it makes holes invisible.

- Doubt how you measure coverage. The first 23% was really 49%, and I got to 90%.

- Do not use “same if contained”. It counts a different product as covered.

- The other side’s entries can be wrong. Among the remainder was one such case.

- Make one judgement for counting and creating. Otherwise the product counted and the product created differ.

- Never use a value shortened for display in processing.

- A hiding process needs a way back, built together.

- Read the terms before importing. Being able to fetch is not being allowed to.

  This is the English version of the original Japanese article (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/coverage-check/).

  More in English

- All English pages (https://koshinstudio.com/en/)

- Toreca Dash (https://koshinstudio.com/en/works/torecadash/)

# Four gaps in monitoring X: posts missing from search, accounts that change hands, a store-finding query, and catching up after an outage

  日本語版 (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/x-monitoring-gaps/)

Written by Koshin (https://koshinstudio.com/en/about/#operator) (web engineer and app engineer) · published 2026-10-17
Development log of the Toreca Dash app / September 2026

  Of my app Toreca Dash’s sources, the fastest and the easiest to miss is stores’ own posts on X (Twitter). Stores announce lotteries and first-come sales on X first. The app patrols registered store accounts regularly.

  On 19 September 2026, four “gaps” in this monitoring turned up in a single day. This is the record.

  Numbers come from my work logs of 19–20 September 2026. Private individuals’ accounts are not named.

## 1. Some posts do not appear in search

  The monitor found posts through X search. But for four stores, lottery announcements did not appear even after fetching 751 posts without any keyword filter, nor per store. X search can omit part of a store’s posts.

  Reading the timeline (the store’s own list of posts) directly (profileTweets) worked.

  The nasty part: a store for which no article can ever be created stays “no track record”. Patrol priority and countermeasures are based on track record, so those stores are never included. What cannot be seen stays unseen (a chicken-and-egg problem).

  The fix: read store timelines in addition to search. But timeline reads cannot be filtered by words and every item read is billed. So stores with a track record are read daily, stores without it weekly, with a cap per store (10 and 8 items).

    Estimate | Value

      Posts per day, stores with a track record | 13.5

      Posts per day, randomly chosen stores | 4.5

      Monthly cost after adding | about $51 (the plan includes $39)

  Cost varies a lot with each store’s posting rate, so always estimate from measurements. It stops automatically once the month passes $62, and an automatic pace check estimates whether all stores can be read daily with the remaining budget, narrowing the stores if not.

## 2. A registered store had quietly stopped being a store

  Two accounts registered as “stores” in the monitoring list were no longer stores. One, registered in August as a branch of a second-hand shop, had become a person’s chatter. The other, registered in May, was an individual info account whose “[PR] lottery sale” posts became articles as if from a store.

  Articles appear as “store primary information”, so wrong information is notified as is.

  The list was checked only once, when registered. Nothing noticed when an account’s owner or use changed.

  The check: match the store name in the list comments against the display name on articles from the last 30 days, by a 2-character overlap. Of 828, I reviewed mismatches by eye and found 2 had become personal. Most mismatches were just “unknown” registrations that became official names, so I decided by eye, not by machine.

## 3. The store-finding search found only 11 of 63 stores

  New stores’ X accounts are found by search. The query was “store name genre name lottery site:x.com”, looking at the top 5 results. Out of 63 stores, it found X for only 11. Aggregators and customers’ posts ranked first and were rejected by the store-name match.

  Among 8 stores whose X account was known, the old method found 5 and the “store name site:x.com” query found 7 (all ranked first).

  But in a dry run right after widening the query, it picked up personal or unrelated accounts, because search-result titles contain the whole post and the match fired on the store name in the body. I changed it to extract only the display-name part of the title. More hits bring more mistakes at the same time. When you change a query, always run a preview and look at each item it picks up.

## 4. Catching up after an outage took half a day

  The data-fetching service’s (Apify) budget ran out, and X monitoring was down for 6 days. When I resumed, in 2 hours it read 185 of 2,866.

  Patrol is a rotation: “stores with a track record every 3 hours, others every 12 hours”. A rotation fits the normal state where everyone is about equally behind. After an outage, lateness is not uniform. Catching up would take more than half a day, and lotteries closing the next day would end before being read.

  For the same reason, newly found accounts joined the middle of the “no track record” list and went unread for up to 12 hours.

  The fix: add to the rotation a slot that reads the longest-unread items, oldest first. Attempt marks are kept separately so items that keep failing do not hog it. I also ran a manual catch-up right after resuming.

## Aside: a “this month only” budget stopped everything twice

  This catch-up was caused by the budget running out. I used to change the cap month by month, “this month only $44”, “automatically go back to $29 on 6 September”. If the value I went back to was below that month’s usage, all X monitoring stopped at the cycle start. It happened twice (28 August and 13 September).

  The decision on 19 September: one monthly cap of $70, and the interval not changed by month (all accounts once per 6 hours). Real monthly cost is about $10 to $18. I do not bring back a month-by-month cap.

## What I learned

> Posts you cannot see cannot be counted.

- Do not rely on search alone. Search does not return everything, and what is invisible raises no complaints.

- Registration is not a one-time check. Owners change. Compare the registered name with the current display name regularly.

- Preview when you change a query. More hits means more mistakes.

- After an outage, catch-up needs its own design. The normal rotation does not suit it.

- Do not change a cost cap by month. Forgetting to restore it, or restoring the wrong value, stops everything.

  This is the English version of the original Japanese article (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/x-monitoring-gaps/).

  More in English

- All English pages (https://koshinstudio.com/en/)

- Toreca Dash (https://koshinstudio.com/en/works/torecadash/)

# When you cannot watch everything quickly: popular 128 of 427 sets run fast, and the fastest lane yields to the budget

  日本語版 (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/hot-lane/)

Written by Koshin (https://koshinstudio.com/en/about/#operator) (web engineer and app engineer) · published 2026-10-17
Development log of the Toreca Dash app / September 2026

  My app Toreca Dash searches shopping sites by set (a release unit of products) to collect first-come and pre-order information. There are 427 sets in all. I would like to watch them all quickly, but there are limits on scraping cost and on calls to external services.

  On the night of 7 September 2026 I decided on a policy, “watch only the popular ones quickly”, and built it. This is a record of what I sped up, what I gave up, and how I protected cost.

  Numbers come from my work log of 7 September 2026.

## Policy: three popular genres, latest and last two years only

  The policy: “for Pokémon cards, ONE PIECE cards and Dragon Ball, the latest sets and the last two years of sets are enough”. Three genres × the last 24 months is 128 sets, about 30% of all 427.

  The original per-set search walked all 427 sets in order, and one lap took different times per site.

     | One lap over 427 sets | Popular lane, 128 sets

      Amazon | 4 hours | every 30 minutes (about 450 s per run)

      Rakuten Books | 24 hours | 22 sets every 10 minutes, one lap per hour

      Rakuten Ichiba | 24 hours | 22 sets every 10 minutes, one lap per hour

      Yahoo! | 8 hours | 128 sets every 2 hours

  The popular lane runs on a separate cursor from the normal lane. Sharing one would disturb the normal lane’s progress.

  Two sites (Amiami and AEON Style) have no concept of a popular lane. They do not search by set but read a list page whole, all at once. There is nothing to narrow; going faster means shortening the interval, which is a cost question.

## Batching them stopped another monitor

  I caused a regression with Rakuten right after adding this, and fixed it on the spot. At first I ran Rakuten as “128 sets in one go every hour”. But Rakuten’s API allows one call per 1.5 seconds shared by all jobs, and the instant sell-out monitor alone uses 30 calls a minute, 75% of the allowance all the time. A batch took over 13 minutes, and meanwhile even the sell-out monitor was skipped as “previous run still going”.

  The same 128 sets per hour, scattered as 22 sets every 10 minutes, makes no pile-up. I also offset the minutes (Rakuten Books lane at :03, :13…, Ichiba lane at :08, :18…). Right afterwards: the sell-out monitor ran 8 times in 9 minutes with 0 skips, average 44.9 s, no worse.

## Fastest lane: popular items truly once a minute

  There was also a request: “I want popular items checked every minute.” That made the third time that day I confirmed what I wrote about before (https://koshinstudio.com/en/notes/interval-vs-delivery/): “runs every minute” is not “checks each item every minute”.

- Rakuten Books sell-out monitor: 62 to 92 items were un-notified, about 30 could be checked per run, one lap 3 minutes. Only 18 of them were in the three popular genres (Pokémon 9, Dragon Ball 5, One Piece 4). Checking those first on every run makes it truly once a minute, at zero cost. The other 44 are about every 3.7 minutes. Advance the cursor only for the rotating part; if popular items advance it, it stops there and other items never get a turn.

- Amazon fastest lane: 28 sets (popular genres, before release or within 60 days after), 10 sets per minute in rotation, one lap about 2.8 minutes. Measured: 27.4 s per run, 0 skips.

  I cannot hit all 28 sets every minute. At 40,320 requests a day, the month would be 1.96 million, above the 1.25 million contract. At 10 sets a minute it is 14,400 a day. In exchange I moved Amazon’s popular lane (128 sets) from 30 to 60 minutes.

    Amazon lane | Target | Cycle

      Fastest | 28 sets before / just after release | about 2.8 min

      Popular | 128 sets, three genres | 1 hour

      Normal | All 427 sets | 4 hours

## What I cannot do, I say I cannot

- Rakuten Ichiba: the sell-out monitor uses 75% of the 1.5-second allowance. Adding every-minute checks would break the monitor. The popular lane (every 20 minutes) is the limit.

- Yahoo!: once a minute is 40,000 calls a day, orders of magnitude over. Also new saves were recently 0. It stays at every 2 hours.

## The fastest lane yields when it exceeds the budget pace

  Amazon is a priority host that passes the scraping service’s daily throttling unconditionally, because it is the lifeline of the first-come race. That is right in itself, but if the every-minute fastest lane also passes unconditionally, Amazon eats the whole allowance and every other site is throttled.

  Rather than fix a count on the safe side, it is more reliable to look at actual consumption and stop automatically. I added a check (isScrapeDoOverPace()) that skips the run if the time-proportional budget pace is exceeded.

  Measured over a 2-minute window: 55 requests, 55 credits, 27.5 credits a minute (about 39,600 a day). The allowance was 1,147,389 remaining and 23 days to reset, 47,392 a day. One trap about window length: measured over 10 minutes it looked like 47.5 credits a minute (68,400 a day). A costly job every 3 hours (25 credits each) happened to fall in that window. Extrapolating from a short window is wrong; check the next day’s daily total.

## What I learned

> When you cannot speed up everything, decide what to speed up and what to slow down in return.

- Narrow the target. 128 of 427; even then only a narrower 18 or 28 can be truly once a minute.

- Do not batch; scatter. The same count with no pile-up does not stop others.

- With a shared allowance, faster for one means slower for another. Decide what to protect first.

- Make the budget yield by itself. Stopping on actual consumption beats a fixed count.

- Do not extrapolate from a short window. Confirm with the daily record.

  This is the English version of the original Japanese article (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/hot-lane/).

  More in English

- All English pages (https://koshinstudio.com/en/)

- Toreca Dash (https://koshinstudio.com/en/works/torecadash/)

# Fixing a gate does not fix existing data: a “tried already” mark, a URL marker and a lookup table

  日本語版 (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/fix-the-existing-data/)

Written by Koshin (https://koshinstudio.com/en/about/#operator) (web engineer and app engineer) · published 2026-10-17
Development log of the Toreca Dash app / August–September 2026

  While developing my app Toreca Dash, I kept getting the same report in the same shape: “I fixed it, but it is not fixed”. The code is fixed, the tests pass, yet the screen still shows the mistake.

  The reason: fixing code does not rewrite data that is already saved. These are three forms of it, with real cases.

  Numbers come from my work logs of 26 August, 3 September and 8 September 2026.

## 1. I loosened a gate, but a “tried already” mark remained (3 September)

  A product-matching gate had a mistake. I fixed it and deployed. Yet 12 of the 32 existing articles stayed wrong.

  The reason was the “skip mark”. When the gate once says “this pairing is wrong”, the article gets a “tried already” mark and is not retried for 7 days. Fixing the judgement does not revisit it while the mark lasts. Among those 12 were 4 open lotteries closing on 5 and 6 September. Lotteries close in days, so waiting for the mark to expire means they vanish. The same day I found the same shape again (a 14-day cooldown in a process that splits into multiple products).

  The fix: before skipping because of a mark, re-check with the current judgement. If the judgement is a pure function that uses neither AI nor external calls, it costs nothing. If you also store “what material I judged with” (for example whether I looked at the image), you can retry only when new material appears.

## 2. A state marker was stored in the URL (3 September)

  Split articles (children) need a marker saying “already split”. At the time I put it in a part of the URL (?_product=product-name): “never split again if this is present”.

  But this project later rewrites application URLs to the store’s official page. The same day I started running that rewrite over everything. Anything stored in the URL is certain to be lost. Of 832 child articles, 111 lost their marker, looked like “parents not yet split”, and were split again. Broken articles pointing at themselves as the “replacement” went from 8 to 14 in 30 minutes. In the past, the same route had once made 1 article into 18.

  The fix was to decide using a field that does not get rewritten, such as splitFromArticleId. The other lesson: on a day you let “a process that only applied to some” run over everything, check what depends on the fields that process rewrites.

## 3. Removing a key from a table does not remove written values (26 August)

  I removed a store chain from the “nearest branch” lookup table. It was gone from the code. But the “nearest branch key” written on articles stayed. The app thought “there is a key, so show a distance”, prepared it and got no answer (the server returns 400 for an unresolvable key). Three articles were stuck forever.

  A change to a table is a change to code; migrating data does not happen automatically. When you remove something from a table, clean the existing data in the same change. This pairs with the mistake of adding a new hidden flag and forgetting to add it to the restore step: that is a miss on the adding side, this is a miss on the removing side.

  Cleaning can reveal new anomalies in audits. Those are real holes that were hidden. I did not restore the key to hide them.

## Five reports of one shape (8 September)

  On 8 September, five of the seven things found by running all 61 audits had the same shape: “a mechanism exists to fix it, but it does not reach the target, or never gets its turn”.

    Symptom | Root

      Opening days mixed into store names (4th report) | The fixer and the gate were different functions; the comment “same yardstick” was false

      A notification opens an article that does not exist (322) | The mark (split) was missing from the target query of the filling job

      Official events still displayed | The rejecting gate existed, but its re-apply never got a turn

      Wrong-unit reference prices (24) | The fix was buried in a 25-job rotation, one lap 2.5 days

      “19 deferred to the next run for time budget” | A cheap fix shared a budget and rotation with an expensive one

  A gate protects only new articles. Fixing existing articles is a separate process, and if that does not run, “fixed but not fixed” repeats. When the same report keeps coming, you have usually fixed the entrance but not the exit (existing data).

  The shared solution was to take “re-apply the save-time gate to existing articles” out of the rotation and run it every time. It reads articles once and passes them through the gate (no AI or external call; at most 20 articles and 50 marks per run).

## What I learned

> When you fix the entrance, fix the exit (existing data) too.

- When you add a gate, check that its re-apply runs every time. A gate protects only new articles.

- Re-check “tried already” marks with the current judgement. Waiting for expiry means the lottery is over.

- Put state markers in fields that are not rewritten. URLs get replaced later.

- When you remove from a table, clean the data. A code change does not move data.

- When a report comes twice, suspect the exit. Fixing the entrance is not enough.

  This is the English version of the original Japanese article (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/fix-the-existing-data/).

  More in English

- All English pages (https://koshinstudio.com/en/)

- Toreca Dash (https://koshinstudio.com/en/works/torecadash/)

URL: https://koshinstudio.com/en/notes/genre-from-catalog/

# Fixing product genre from the official catalogue: three dry runs took 13 changes down to 4

  日本語版 (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/genre-from-catalog/)

Written by Koshin (https://koshinstudio.com/en/about/#operator) (web engineer and app engineer) · published 2026-10-17
Development log of the Toreca Dash app / September 2026

  In my app Toreca Dash a report said: “this product being treated as a Pokémon card is wrong in the first place”. The product was “Winning enemy! Reversal, the Oni’s ∞ Dispectar!!”. It is a Duel Masters product, but had been registered as a Pokémon card product and shown in the Pokémon feed.

  The fix was “make the official catalogue the source of truth for genre”. But before applying it in bulk I needed three dry runs before it was safe. This is that process.

  Numbers come from my work log of 11 September 2026.

## Why a Duel Masters product became Pokémon

  Store X accounts are monitored as “Pokémon card” accounts, so an article’s genre becomes its product’s genre. This product’s name has neither the game’s name nor a product code. The two existing judgements (guess from words in the name, guess from the product code) could answer neither.

  The official catalogue lists it as “DM26-RP3 Duel Masters TCG Reverse Card chapter 3 Winning enemy! Reversal, the Oni’s ∞ Dispectar!!”. Like the product name, image and price, genre too belongs to the official source. I added a judgement “decide genre from the official catalogue” and put the same judgement in both the entrance (creating products) and the re-apply step (fixing existing products).

## Dry run 1: nine correct products were about to be moved to another game

  The first rule was “if the name is wholly contained in a set name of exactly one genre, use that genre”. A dry run (results only, no writes) gave 13 to fix. Nine correct Weiss Schwarz products would have been moved to Union Arena.

    Run | Rule | To fix | What was in it

      1 | Name wholly contained in one genre’s set | 13 | 9 correct Weiss products moved to Union Arena

      2 | + ambiguity checked on the work name with form words removed | 9 | 5 Weiss products still misfired

      3 | + only when the official set name itself names the game or a code | 4 | 0 misfires

## The real cause: the official list does not cover old sets

  Misfires came from the official list not including older sets (Weiss Schwarz has 64, only recent ones). Also a set name that is only a form word plus a work name, such as “Booster Pack Chainsaw Man”, does not identify the game, because the same work’s cards appear in several games.

  So I trust a match only when the set name contains a game name such as “Duel Masters TCG” or “ONE PIECE”, or a code only that genre uses such as [SB02], [EVX13] or DM26-RP3.

  The four left were all correct fixes:

  pokemon    → onepiece     "Heroines Edition"        (ONE PIECE ... [EB-03])
pokemon    → duelmasters  "Winning enemy! Reversal..." (the reported one)
yugioh     → dragonball   "MANGA BOOSTER 02"        ([SB02])
dragonball → gundam       "Premium Card Collection 02" ([EVX13])

## One more: a product name written across lines was treated as “not written”

  The same day another automatic report came in: “rejected a match whose product-name fingerprint did not match”. Stores’ X posts write product names across several lines.

  [On sale today]
○ Union Arena
Advanced Deck
∟ BLEACH Thousand-Year Blood War
Limit one per person

* Booster Pack "BLEACH Thousand-Year Blood War Vol.3" is
sold by lottery. Only winners may buy.
  The match code has a rule: “if the chosen product name appears whole in the title, say nothing”. But it did not strip the leading “∟”, so it judged the name as not whole in the title. It then used another product in the same post (“Booster Pack BLEACH Thousand-Year Blood War Vol.3”) as grounds to reject a correct match.

  Several products in one post is normal. The fix was to add continuation marks (∟ └ ┗ ├ ┣ ⇒ → ▶ >) to the comparison-only normaliser. It is called from 6 places, so one fix applies to all. I confirmed on real data that a rejection becomes an acceptance.

## What I learned

> One dry run is not enough.

- An official list is not complete. Do not stop at “trust it if it is listed”; narrow to “only when it names itself”.

- Dry-run before you write. 13 in run 1, 4 in run 3, and 0 misfires.

- Put the same judgement at the entrance and the re-apply step. One of them alone leaves a gap.

- Normalise writing variants before comparing. One “∟” dropped a correct match.

  This is the English version of the original Japanese article (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/genre-from-catalog/).

- Toreca Dash (https://koshinstudio.com/en/works/torecadash/)

# 393 “work-name-only” products from an official list: the name field did not contain the product form

  日本語版 (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/catalog-seed-393/)

Written by Koshin (https://koshinstudio.com/en/about/#operator) (web engineer and app engineer) · published 2026-10-17
Development log of the Toreca Dash app / September 2026

  The product list of my app Toreca Dash is partly built from official site lists. Counting products created by that import per day, I saw 502 in one day, against the usual 1 to 10.

  Looking inside, 379 were Weiss Schwarz, and the names looked like this:

  GA Bunko
Makai Senki Disgaea 4
Goddess of Victory: NIKKE
Love Live! Nijigasaki High School Idol Club
  All of them were names of works, not names of products. This is the cause, and a side effect that appeared after the clean-up.

  Numbers come from my work log of 7 September 2026.

## The cause: the product form was outside the name

  On the official list page, the name field (products__name) holds only the work name. The product form (booster pack, trial deck) is in the category (part of the page URL).

    Category | Real data in the name field

      booster-pack | “Azur Lane Vol.3”, “Stellasora”, “anemoi”

      trial-deck | “Girls und Panzer Oarai Girls Academy”, “GA Bunko”

  The right product name carries the form, like “Trial Deck GA Bunko”. It then matches existing correct products such as “Booster Pack D4DJ Groovy Mix”.

## The fix: at the entrance, and for what was already made

  Entrance: add the form from the category (trial-deck becomes trial deck, booster-pack becomes booster pack, and so on). If the form cannot be decided (“others”), do not add it and do not create the product.

  Existing items: I made a clean-up tool. By default it only previews; it deletes with delete=true. It deletes only items for which all four are true:

- created from the official list,

- no form word in the name,

- no articles attached,

- no official price and no image.

  The preview found 393. After the run, products went from 811 to 418. One, “[Oshi no Ko] Vol.3”, has articles attached, so I kept it. Over-deletion draws no complaints, so I keep the conditions strict.

  After cleaning I re-imported the official list and re-registered 328 Weiss Schwarz entries with correct names (form attached, like “Trial Deck Is the Order a Rabbit??”). Zero entries lack a form word.

## Why no audit caught it

  The name audit looks for “unnatural product names”: symbols, line breaks, URLs. Proper Japanese work names do not look unnatural. “Love Live! Nijigasaki High School Idol Club” is a perfectly good name.

  The other gap: there was no audit that counts. Counting “products created per day” would have made 502 obvious. If you only look at what is shown, things that quietly increase are invisible.

## A side effect: alias collisions from 0 pairs to 250

  Adding 328 correctly named products caused a new problem. Products have alternative names (aliases). An existing product’s alias, “Booster Pack Is the Order a Rabbit??”, collided with the new official-name product. The audit that counts aliases claimed by two or more products went from 0 pairs to 250.

  I ran the repair tool the audit points to, previewing first. The rule is “keep the one that uses the name as its official name”; only the other product loses it. 253 ambiguous aliases (220 products) were removed, and the audit returned to 0.

## What I learned

> After a change that grows the catalogue, run the audits again.

- Check what a source field really contains on real data. The “name” field does not necessarily hold the product name.

- Count how many are created per day. 502 would have been obvious.

- When deleting, require all conditions. Keep anything that has articles.

- More names mean more collisions. If you fix the entrance and stop, the next person sees 250 in an audit that should be 0.

  This is the English version of the original Japanese article (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/catalog-seed-393/).

# Online play that trusts nothing the client says: the server decides moves, clocks and results

  日本語版 (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/negaeri-online/)

Written by Koshin (https://koshinstudio.com/en/about/#operator) (web engineer and app engineer) · published 2026-10-17
Development log of Negaeri Shogi / September 2026

  Negaeri Shogi (https://koshinstudio.com/en/works/negaeri-shogi/) has online play against strangers, with no sign-up or login. Press a button and you are matched with someone else who is waiting.

  The first rule I set for an online game was: trust nothing the client says. A client can be rewritten by its owner. It can send lies: “the board is like this”, “I have 2 minutes left”, “I won”. This article records how I built the server so those lies do not matter. Numbers and mechanisms are the real values in the server code.

  This is a record of the mechanism. Balance between human players is still not verified enough (see how I set the rules by AI-vs-AI play (https://koshinstudio.com/en/notes/negaeri-balance/)).

## Principle: the server decides; the client only asks

  A client can send only three kinds of message:

- join: join this match (with a signed identity token).

- move: play this move.

- resign: resign.

  It cannot send the board, the remaining time or the result. A received move is checked against the server’s own board by the rules engine, the same file the screen uses. Because the rules are written in one place, a move the screen allows can never be “illegal” on the server.

## One match = one small server

  The server runs on Cloudflare Workers. One match is handled by one Durable Object (a small server that keeps state), and both players connect to it over a WebSocket. The match’s progress (moves and clocks) is saved the moment each move is committed.

  A Durable Object sleeps when idle. When it wakes it replays the saved moves from the start to rebuild the board. Saving only the moves is less likely to drift than saving the board.

## What the server does when a move arrives

- Check for a timeout first. If the player to move has used all their time, the move is not accepted and they lose on time.

- Check whose turn it is. A move out of turn gets “it is not your turn”.

- Validate with the rules. An illegal move makes that player lose (reason: illegal move).

- Apply the move. Advance the board, append the move, advance the clock, save.

- Tell both players. The move, the order of flipped pieces, the chain count and the new clocks.

  An illegal move is not dropped silently; it loses the game.

## Only the server holds the clock

  Each player gets 3 minutes, plus 5 seconds per move (Fischer clock). The clock lives only on the server; the time on the screen is just a display of what the server sent.

  // when a move is committed
const used = now - clock.turnStartedAt;
clock.remaining[mover] = Math.max(0, clock.remaining[mover] - used) + INCREMENT_MS;
clock.turnStartedAt = now;
  Subtract the time used, add 5 seconds, start the other side’s turn. Math.max(0, …) keeps it from going below 0.

  The other problem is who notices a timeout when nobody moves. If the opponent sends nothing, the server does nothing. So I use an alarm (the server is woken at a given time). The next wake time is the earlier of “the moment the player to move runs out” and “the moment the disconnect grace ends”, and at least 1 second ahead.

## A disconnect gets 30 seconds

  Mobile connections drop. Losing on a momentary dropout would be harsh, so even after a disconnect the server waits 30 seconds. The opponent is told that the player left and how long the wait is. If the player returns in time, play resumes; the server resends all moves and clock state (a sync) so the screen catches up. If not, they lose on time.

  If the same person reopens the same match on another screen, the older connection is closed, so two screens cannot send different moves.

## Identifying people without sign-up

  With no login, the server must prove “you are that ID”. It issues an ID and signs it with a secret key (HMAC-SHA256), giving a token of the form “ID.signature”. The client stores it.

  To pose as another ID you need that ID’s valid signature, which you cannot make without the key. Signatures are compared with a comparison that checks every character to the end. An ordinary comparison stops at the first different character, and the timing difference can leak the signature.

  The token is valid only while it stays on the device. Clearing the device’s data makes you a new person. It is the trade-off for not requiring registration.

## Matchmaking: start close in rating, widen the longer you wait

  It matches players with close ratings. It starts at ±100 and widens the allowed gap by 100 every 10 seconds of waiting: a compromise between not making people wait and matching similar strength.

  Two players are paired if the gap fits either player’s allowed range, so the one waiting longer takes priority and no one waits forever. With several waiting, it goes from the longest wait and picks the closest rating.

  The lower-rated player gets the first move. The first move is slightly stronger, so the weaker player holds the stronger side, partly cancelling the gap.

## Ratings: Elo, using pre-match numbers

  Ratings use Elo, starting at 1500. The expected score is:

  1 / (1 + 10 ** ((opponentRating - myRating) / 400))
  The step size (K) is large while you have few games: 40 up to 30 games, 20 up to 100, then 10, so ratings approach true strength quickly.

  What I took care over: do not update the two ratings one after the other. Updating one first and then computing the other uses the opponent’s updated rating, which is unfair. Both use pre-match ratings.

  Only players with 10 or more games appear on the ranking, to avoid someone playing once and parking at a lucky rating.

## How I check it

- Unit tests: 126 tests cover rules, AI, clocks, rating, matchmaking and signatures.

- End-to-end tests: there are tests that open two browsers and make an online match happen, and tests that connect directly to the server.

  Not yet verified: behaviour with many strangers playing, and whether the first-player edge (61% in AI-vs-AI play (https://koshinstudio.com/en/notes/negaeri-balance/)) is the same for humans.

## What I learned

> Everything a client reports is a request. The server decides.

- The server holds the clock, the board and the result. Anything you give the client can be rewritten.

- Use the same rules for the screen and the server. Separate copies drift apart.

- Assume connections break. Decide the wait and the restore beforehand.

- Updating in sequence is unfair. Compute ratings from pre-match numbers.

  This is the English version of the original Japanese article (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/negaeri-online/).

  More in English

- All English pages (https://koshinstudio.com/en/)

- Negaeri Shogi (https://koshinstudio.com/en/works/negaeri-shogi/)

# “The same application page” does not mean “the same store”: 52 articles showed another store’s name

  日本語版 (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/same-page-not-same-store/)

Written by Koshin (https://koshinstudio.com/en/about/#operator) (web engineer and app engineer) · published 2026-10-17
Development log of the Toreca Dash app / September 2026

  In my app Toreca Dash a bug report said: “to users it looks like a different store’s lottery”. An article for a Sendai station store showed as “Shinjuku South Exit store”, and an article for a Hachioji flagship showed as “Noshiro store”. 52 articles were affected.

  The cause was a wrong premise: “the same application page means the same store.”

  Numbers come from my work log of 7 September 2026.

## The symptom: store names of other stores

  Articles carried the name of a different branch of the same chain. A user opens “the Sendai store’s lottery” and the text says Shinjuku. 52 articles were like that.

## The cause: the same page is not the same store

  A job unified the store name and deadline across articles that share an application page. Same lottery, same deadline; same store, same name, I assumed. It copied the highest-quality article’s store name to everyone in the group.

  The premise did not hold. On real data:

    Application page | Stores sharing it

      A page (1) | 15 separate stores (Sendai, Hamamatsu, Maebashi, Shiwa, Gamagori, Hiroshima and more)

      A page (2) | 9 branches of one chain

      A page (3) | One shop and three other chains (not even the same chain)

  Chains often use one application page for all stores. The same page does not mean the same store.

  The same accident had already happened on the hiding side, and a guard existed there (the 51-branch case of one chain). I had forgotten to add it to the name-copying side. The same fix had not been applied to every entrance that uses the same judgement.

## A coordinates-only guard was not enough

  My first guard was “if coordinates disagree, they are different stores”. But for a group where only one article has coordinates, the “definitely different places” test returns false and passes. In a dry run (no writes), shops of three different chains were about to be rewritten as one store.

  The lasting fix was to reverse the logic: “unify only when confirmed to be the same place”, not “do not unify when confirmed different”. Only when both have coordinates and they match. If coordinates are missing or differ, I respect each article’s own name. Deadlines are still unified, since they belong to the same lottery on the same page.

## Restoring the 52 articles

  I had not saved the original names. The clue was a field this job never touches (category), set when an article is created from its own source (the store’s X account or the aggregator row). I checked all 52 by eye, and category matched the source.

  Coordinates could not serve as evidence. They are derived from the store name, so after a rewrite they were the coordinates of the wrong name (category was Sapporo Station but coordinates were Shinjuku). So I discarded coordinates too and put them back to be derived again.

- 51 in a dry run, then the real run.

- Afterwards, 0 new overwrites (the guard works).

- Only 2 displayed articles where name and category differed, both just different spellings of one store.

## A bonus bug: items that could not enter the queue

  Trying to re-derive coordinates, none of 4 articles got their turn. The location fixer has two queues:

    Queue | Contents

      Front (60 at a time) | Articles that want coordinates

      Retry (a 300-item window) | 658 measured, of which only 34 truly lacked coordinates

  The retry queue also held items that had been solved (success wrote the flag as false and left it in the queue). 624 finished articles filled the window, so the 34 that needed work never got a turn.

  The fix: when solved, delete the flag. It sits in neither queue.

## What I learned

> Before assuming “the same”, confirm “the same”.

- The same link does not mean the same store. Shared pages are normal.

- Unify only what you have confirmed is the same. If you cannot confirm, do not touch it.

- Apply a fix to every entrance that uses the same judgement. Adding it to one leaves the other.

- If you did not save the original, restore from a field you did not touch, and check it by eye, one by one.

- Setting a flag to false is not deleting it. It stays in the queue.

  This is the English version of the original Japanese article (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/same-page-not-same-store/).

  More in English

- Toreca Dash (https://koshinstudio.com/en/works/torecadash/)

# When first-come sales start, the site becomes a waiting-room page: a 15 KB notice slipped through an 8,000-byte gate

  日本語版 (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/waiting-room/)

Written by Koshin (https://koshinstudio.com/en/about/#operator) (web engineer and app engineer) · published 2026-10-17
Development log of the Toreca Dash app / September 2026

  My app Toreca Dash reads shopping-site pages to collect first-come and lottery information. As I wrote in an earlier article (https://koshinstudio.com/en/notes/blocked-page/), my “was it fetched?” check had a hole and treated a notice page as success. On the very day I fixed it (7 September 2026), I found another hole of the same kind in a different shape.

  And it occurred at the moment when missing something matters most.

  Numbers come from my work log of 7 September 2026.

## When first-come sales start, the site becomes a waiting-room page

  A report came: “AEON Style Online seems to have first-come sales too”, “it seems to have started at exactly 14:00”. So I tried fetching at that moment.

    Method | Result

      Plain request | 403 (blocked by bot protection)

      Scraping service, cheap setting | 200, 15,188 bytes, title “Notice: heavy access”

      Scraping service, super | 200, 15,188 bytes, same

      Scraping service, super + render | 200, 15,459 bytes, same

  The instant a first-come sale starts, the whole site becomes a waiting-room page, and every setting returns the same notice.

## A 15 KB notice slipped through an 8,000-byte gate

  The “not fetched” check I had added earlier that day looked for a JavaScript notice inside pages under 8,000 bytes. Large legitimate pages also contain the same sentence.

  This waiting-room page is about 15 KB. It passed the gate and was read as “fetch succeeded, 0 products”. It failed silently at the moment I most needed it.

  The fix: look at the title, not the size. If the title contains “heavy access” or “we will guide you in order”, treat it as a failure. I limited it to the title so legitimate pages that merely mention those words are not caught.

  I also changed the frequency from every 3 hours to every 15 minutes. At about 21 credits a run it is costly, but about 6,000 credits a day stays within 92% of the remaining balance.

## Two more causes of slowness found the same day

  Amazon’s 13 minutes were AI screening, not fetching. The Amazon monitor ran every 30 minutes, one scan took 13 minutes and the worst delay was about 43 minutes. The meter showed the time went to AI screening of new listings (421 a day, about ¥10). Fetching itself cost only 1,047 credits a day. The cause was handling 15 genres one at a time. They are independent, so I ran 4 in parallel, with a 10-minute interval and 8-minute runs. AI screening runs only for new listings, so cost does not rise with patrol frequency.

  Even when found fast, 17% were not notified. Finding things sooner means nothing if notifications stop afterwards. Counting what was delivered showed another hole (see the article on counting notifications (https://koshinstudio.com/en/notes/interval-vs-delivery/)).

## What I learned

> A hole in a judgement widens at the most important moment.

- A notice page has more than one shape. Short ones and big waiting-room pages. Size cannot tell them apart.

- Changing where you look reduces collateral. Title, not body, so legitimate pages are not caught.

- When a report arrives, measure at that time, on the spot. “It started at 14:00” was the last chance to reproduce.

- Check where slow time really goes. Amazon’s 13 minutes were serial AI screening, not fetching.

  This is the English version of the original Japanese article (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/waiting-room/).

  More in English

- All English pages (https://koshinstudio.com/en/)

- Toreca Dash (https://koshinstudio.com/en/works/torecadash/)

# Before widening concurrency slots: widening a 2-core server from 8 to 14, and the earlier conclusion that was half wrong

  日本語版 (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/concurrency-slots/)

Written by Koshin (https://koshinstudio.com/en/about/#operator) (web engineer and app engineer) · published 2026-10-17
Development log of the Toreca Dash app / September 2026

  The back end of my app Toreca Dash runs over 200 scheduled jobs on one small server (2 cores, 3.8 GB of memory). The number of jobs that can run at once is capped: the concurrency slots.

  On 7 September 2026, when I shortened some intervals to speed up first-come monitoring, the monitor I most wanted fast was slowed by waiting for a slot. I raised the slots from 8 to 11 and then 14. This is the record of that decision and of what to look at.

  Numbers come from my work log of 7 September 2026.

## 8 slots were not enough

  To speed up first-come monitoring I shortened several intervals. Then the one-minute “instant sell-out monitor” started being skipped, because all 8 slots were full.

     | 8 slots (after shortening) | 11 slots

      Queue length | 17–29 | 0

      Running at once | pinned at 8 | 6 / 11 (room)

      Monitor skips | 6 per 10 min | 1 per 10 min

      Load average | 1.62 | 1.24

      Memory | 1,161 MB | 667 MB

  With 11 slots the queue was 0 and load and memory fell. Most jobs only wait for network replies and use no CPU. The cap was the slots, not the CPU.

  The slot value lives only in a server settings file (runner.env) and never enters git, because the deploy script does not send it. Looking at the repository would not show this change, so I wrote it down and kept a backup of the old value.

## “Only 2 cores, so no more” was half wrong

  Later I added a lane for popular sets and a fastest lane. Concurrency pinned at 11, the queue grew to 15 and the monitor was skipped twice (effective interval 1.0 to 1.4 minutes).

- 2 cores, load 1.66, 83% of them.

- Long Rakuten jobs hold a slot while sleeping on the API’s 1.5-second wait: stock recheck 240 s, marketplace 181 s, new listings 110 s, stock 104 s.

- They use no CPU yet consume slots, the hardest culprit to see.

  At the time I concluded “with 2 cores, widening the slots would just slow everything” and reduced the Rakuten popular lanes.

     | After adding | After reducing

      Concurrency | pinned at 11 | 9–11

      Queue | up to 15 | 0–1

      Monitor skips | 2 per 10 min | 0

      Monitor effective interval | 1.4 min | 1.0 min

      Load | 1.66 | 1.25

  That conclusion turned out half wrong. The Rakuten jobs holding slots are asleep on the API wait and use no CPU. More slots only means “more can sleep at once”, not more CPU contention. I measured again with 11 and 14:

     | 11 slots | 14 slots

      Monitor skips | 1 per 5 min | 0 per 6.7 min

      Effective interval | 1.3 min | 1.0 min

      Load | 1.25 | 1.25 (unchanged)

## The deciding question: CPU-bound or waiting?

- If waiting jobs hold the slots, widen them, after checking load (uptime) does not rise.

- If CPU-bound jobs hold them, widening slows everything.

  Two places to look: the queue length (queued in the health check; if it is always at least 1 there is no spare), and the average run time per job, longest first. If long Rakuten-API jobs top the list, they are the ones sleeping on slots.

  That day I made the same regression four times: Amazon every 5 minutes, Amazon-like store every 5 minutes, batched Rakuten popular lanes, Rakuten popular lanes every 10 minutes. Each time I meant to speed up and instead ate slots and slowed the one I cared about.

## What I learned

> Do not count slots; look at what holds them.

- A job whose run time ≥ its interval occupies a slot. The faster it goes, the more others wait.

- Measure what the limit really is. CPU or slots? Look at load and memory.

- A previous conclusion can be half wrong. “2 cores, so no” did not apply to waiting jobs.

- Record settings that are not in git. A value only on the server is invisible in the repository.

- To speed one thing up, slow another down. Decide what to protect first.

  This is the English version of the original Japanese article (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/concurrency-slots/).

  More in English

- All English pages (https://koshinstudio.com/en/)

- Toreca Dash (https://koshinstudio.com/en/works/torecadash/)

URL: https://koshinstudio.com/en/notes/split-mixups/

# Three mix-ups in splitting one article into products: a child treated as a parent, a shared link pointing to another store, a name owned by two products

  日本語版 (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/split-mixups/)

Written by Koshin (https://koshinstudio.com/en/about/#operator) (web engineer and app engineer) · published 2026-10-17
Development log of the Toreca Dash app / September 2026

  My app Toreca Dash has a process that splits a store announcement into one article per product. If one announcement says “lotteries for Pokémon card A and B”, it makes an article for A and one for B. I call the split articles children and the original the parent.

  Around this process I found three mix-ups. In each, a real lottery disappeared and nothing showed on screen.

  Numbers come from my work logs of September 2026 (including 5 and 20 September).

## 1. Parent-level processing was applied to a child again (20 September)

  In a broad check I found that 60 lotteries (23 stores) closing at 23:59 that day were all missing from the feed.

  A child keeps the parent’s flyer image and the parent’s title (splitFromTitle). A job that re-asks about articles with several products looked at a child, read it as “9 products”, left the child’s product field empty and rewrote it as “9 items”. The next day a job that tidies generic articles (those that point to no particular product) judged it “a generic article with no product” and hid it.

  The target product IDs were the same as the existing siblings, so zero new articles were made. Only that product vanished.

  The same root cause hit a second place: the check for result announcements and winner notices missed children because a child’s title is only the product name, and the body (the parent’s title) did not reach the check (16 articles).

  The fix: when adding a job that collects, judges or hides articles, always decide to exclude children (articles with splitFromArticleId) or pass the parent title as body. The marker for “this is a child” is a field on the article, not a part of the URL, because URL markers are lost when application links are rewritten.

## 2. Looking up the parent by link alone returned another store’s article

  Ten two-product announcements from one store chain were never split. The function that finds the parent looked it up by link alone.

  That chain’s stores share one page, 13 stores with the same link. A link-only lookup hit one of:

- an ID fixed by the link alone,

- the first of the articles with that link,

- a child whose marker was lost in a link rewrite (it has the parent’s link).

  As a result it split another store’s article, or a child, again and again. The log showed “split into 2 products” for the same parent each time.

  A link is not a key that identifies a store. Shared pages, quotes and aggregator posts give several articles the same link. The fix: when looking up by link, add site and store name to the condition, and never take a child as a parent. “If the log shows the same parent ID again and again, suspect it” is now a lesson.

## 3. A name claimed by two products identifies neither (5 September)

  Products have alternative names. “30th CELEBRATION BOX” was an alias of both the expansion pack “30th CELEBRATION” and a different product, “30th CELEBRATION FUTURISTIC BOX”.

  That name identifies neither. If an AI sees it as a candidate, the result depends on which one it picked at that moment. 25 displayed articles were shown under the other product’s name.

  Counting, such “names claimed by two or more products” numbered 267 pairs and 321 articles.

  The same shape: a step that cut store names “before the ＠” merged three branches of one shop into one store and folded two of them away as duplicates every day.

  The fix: whenever a system identifies something by name, count whether two or more things claim that name. An audit keeps it at zero. Keep a name only when it is mechanically decidable (exactly one product uses it as its official name); otherwise remove it from all. Put the same judgement at the entrance and in the cleaner, or what you remove is added back.

## What I learned

> A split-off article is not the original. A name works as a key only if it has one owner.

- Do not re-run the original’s processing on derived items. Keep the child marker in a field of the article.

- A link is not a key. Also use site and store name.

- Count the owners of a name. A name claimed by two identifies nothing.

- When you add a job that hides things, count whether a replacement is really displayed. Looking only at the hidden side cannot show over-deletion.

  This is the English version of the original Japanese article (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/split-mixups/).

- Toreca Dash (https://koshinstudio.com/en/works/torecadash/)
