# Four things that stopped my iOS app before App Review: iPad screenshots, ITMS-91064, account deletion, reporting posts

  日本語版 (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/torecadash-review/)

Written by Koshin (https://koshinstudio.com/en/about/#operator) (web engineer and app engineer) · published 2026-10-09
Development log of Torecadash / October 2026

  When I tried to submit my iOS app Torecadash to App Review, I was stopped before submitting several times: things caught by Apple’s automated checks, things caught on the submission screen, and things I found by checking against the guidelines. From my commit record, here are four.

  The result of review is not included in this article.

## 1. I was asked for iPad screenshots

  When I tried to submit for review in App Store Connect, it stopped me with “You must upload a screenshot for 13-inch iPad displays.” The project settings had been iPhone and iPad (1,2) from the beginning.

  But there was no sign that I had built it with iPad in mind. Device checks and layout adjustments were all on iPhone. Submitting it unverified as “iPad supported” was a risk, so I changed it to iPhone only (1).

## 2. “Invalid Binary” in the automated check (ITMS-91064)

  Build 877 was rejected by Apple’s automated review as an “invalid binary.” The cause was in the privacy manifest (PrivacyInfo.xcprivacy): I had written that it tracks (NSPrivacyTracking=true), but the list of tracking domains (NSPrivacyTrackingDomains) was empty. Apple’s check rejects this combination as a contradiction.

  The app shows AdMob ads (banner, native, app-open) personalized after ATT consent. It does track, so “true” was correct. What needed fixing was the empty domain list. But Google does not publish an official list of domains for AdMob. So I added widely used ad-serving domains (googlesyndication.com, googleadservices.com, doubleclick.net, google.com). I confirmed that a Release build passes.

## 3. Account deletion (Guideline 5.1.1(v))

  An app that lets you create an account must let you delete it from within the app. The deletion also removes the user’s map posts (sighting reports) and their related data (owner, reports, flags, thanks). For people signed in with Apple, the app re-authenticates with Apple, then deletes on the server and revokes the token. I also matched the explanation in the settings screen and the privacy policy to the real behavior.

  In addition, deleting the account does not cancel a subscription. I added this to the settings text and to the deletion confirmation screen (as a review requirement).

## 4. User-generated posts (Guideline 1.2)

  Map posts can be written freely by users. Until then there were only format checks such as length and coordinate range, and nothing that rejected by content. So I added a simple banned-word check to three free-text fields (shop name, product name, note). If it matches, the post is created but starts in a pending-review state.

  One more thing. Reports of posts would go unnoticed unless I myself remembered the admin screen’s URL and opened it. I added the count of items pending review to my daily operations notice so they are not overlooked.

## What I learned

> Review is not something you fail after submitting; half of it is found by checking before you submit.

- Of the four, two (iPad, ITMS-91064) were stopped by a machine. The other two (deletion, posts) I found by reading the guidelines and checking myself.

- “Do not submit what is unverified” was faster and safer than “support everything” (the iPad case).

  This article is written from my commit record (September 16 to October 6, 2026).

  This is the English version of the original Japanese article (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/torecadash-review/).

  More in English

- All English pages (https://koshinstudio.com/en/)

# I re-measured a “nothing can be done” assumption and scraping cost dropped to one eighth

  日本語版 (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/scrape-cost/)

Written by Koshin (https://koshinstudio.com/en/about/#operator) (web engineer and app engineer) · published 2026-10-09
Development log of Torecadash / October 2026

  My iOS app Torecadash regularly visits sales pages on online shops and collects lottery and first-come sale information. Pages are fetched through an external service (Scrape.do), and each fetch setting uses a different number of credits. For one site, I re-measured something I had accepted as “it cannot be helped,” and it became 3 times faster using about one eighth of the credits. This is from my commit record.

  This is a development log of the app. I do not write amounts of money, only numbers of credits.

## The reason for “it cannot be helped” was cost

  I thought the fetch interval for two sites, AEON Style Online and Amiami, could not be shortened. The reason was that fetching was expensive. In other words, a conclusion based on an old unit price. I decided to measure it again.

## Fetching the same page with three settings

  There are three levels of fetch settings: a plain fetch (1 credit), render in a browser and then fetch (render, 5 credits), and render through a stronger route (super + render, 25 credits). I fetched AEON’s list page with all three and compared contents, two pages three times each.

    Setting | Credits | Size (bytes) | Products | Prices

    Plain | 1 | 649,734 | 20 | 25

    render | 5 | 663,026 | 20 | 25

    super + render | 25 | 669,510 | 20 | 25

  All three returned exactly the same products and prices. So rendering was a complete waste. I had been paying 25 credits for something that 1 credit was enough for.

## The fix

- Try the cheap setting first. For AEON, fetch plainly first. Only when the “access is busy” page that appears at the start of a first-come sale comes back does it escalate automatically to a stronger setting.

- Interval from 15 minutes to 5 minutes. Every 5 minutes is 288 times a day. For 2 pages, that is 576 credits. Before, it was about 4,600 credits a day (as stated in the commit). It is 3 times faster and uses about one eighth.

- I applied the same measured result to Amiami. Removing rendering took one fetch from 5 credits to 1, saving about 1,200 credits a day.

  But for Amiami I kept the interval at 15 minutes. That day it had hit timeouts twice, and one run took 284 seconds. Fetching overall was getting crowded, so I decided not to touch it. What I measured was “is rendering needed,” not “is it safe to shorten the interval.”

## What I learned

> When was the number behind “it cannot be helped” measured?

- Re-measure old conclusions. Unit prices, settings and how sites are built all change. “AEON cannot be helped” turned out not to be true when measured.

- Strong settings tend to get added “just in case.” Whether they are needed can be seen by comparing results. If the results are the same, the cheaper one is enough.

- When you fix one thing, check the other conditions. The same measurement fixed Amiami’s setting, but I left its interval because of a separate issue (timeouts).

  The numbers in this article come from my commit record (September 7, 2026). “4,600” is as written in the commit and is a little off from the calculation of 25 credits × 2 pages × 96 runs (every 15 minutes) = 4,800.

  This is the English version of the original Japanese article (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/scrape-cost/).

  More in English

- All English pages (https://koshinstudio.com/en/)

# A bulk update hit “all articles”: count before you write, and break your tests to prove they work

  日本語版 (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/bulk-accident/)

Written by Koshin (https://koshinstudio.com/en/about/#operator) (web engineer and app engineer) · published 2026-10-09
Development log of Torecadash / October 2026

  In my iOS app Torecadash, a new job that fixes article status in bulk hit every article, including ones I never meant to target, the first time I ran it. 18 items from other sites were wrongly restored to visible. This is how I fixed the accident, and how I checked that the test I built afterward to close the same hole actually works, from my hand-over notes.

  This is a development log of the app.

## What the job was for

  The app has a “price gate” that checks whether a listing’s price is reasonable (I wrote about it in another article (https://koshinstudio.com/en/notes/fail-open/)). Among articles hidden by this gate only because of price, I added a job that restores those that were actually correct and had been hidden because of a product mix-up. The condition for restoring is “the correct product’s list price matches the listing price.”

## The accident: it hit all articles

  At first this job hit all articles without distinguishing the source. As a result, 18 articles from other sites (Amazon, Card Labo, Ministop and others) were restored to visible. They should have stayed hidden.

  There were two fixes.

- Narrow the scope. I limited the job to articles from that source only (those whose site identifier starts with that source).

- Put back what I had restored. I identified the 18 wrongly restored articles from the status history (statusHistory) and put them back to their original state (hidden, rejected by price).

  But there was something I could not get back for these 18. The job had overwritten the original list-price field with the listing price. The value stays as the listing price.

  The cause was that I had not counted the target range before writing. My notes say so: “count the target range before a bulk write.”

## Building tests to close the same hole

  To make sure the problems found in that day’s inspection (wrong splitting of 9-pack sets, single cards slipping in, non-card products slipping in) never happen again, I built tests: 66 cases in catalog-guards.test.js, and all six test files together can be run in one procedure (run-all.sh).

  I also added warnings to my daily operations notice: when the miss rate of matching falls below the criteria (Chusen Zukan 80%, Pokechu 75%, X roundup 75%), when nothing has run for 30 hours, and when single cards or non-card names appear in the product list. The judgments are pure functions with no side effects, so once things are fixed, the warning disappears by itself on the next run.

## Breaking it to check that the tests work

  You cannot tell whether a test works just by writing it. A test that always passes may protect nothing. So I took a copy of the production code and removed its rules one at a time to confirm the tests fail.

- Remove one rule (break it).

- Run the tests.

- If they fail, the test is protecting that rule.

  With this procedure, I tried 6 kinds of modification, and the tests failed for all 6 (all were detected).

  I also wrote down an operating rule: if I touch functions/index.js, I always run all the tests before deploying.

## What I learned

> Count before a bulk write. Break the test to prove it.

- Before writing, count “how many it will hit.” If you run it without a preview, you notice the range was wrong only after it has finished writing.

- Write in a form you can undo. I could restore the 18 because I could identify them from the history. The overwritten field, though, cannot be restored.

- Prefer a test that fails when broken to a test that passes. Only after removing a rule and seeing it fail can I trust the test.

  This article is written from my hand-over notes (§272) (October 7, 2026). The counts are as written in the notes.

  This is the English version of the original Japanese article (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/bulk-accident/).

  More in English

- All English pages (https://koshinstudio.com/en/)

# Pokémon card sleeves and loaders: sizes and what “pt” means

  日本語版 (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/card-supplies-guide/)

Written by Koshin (https://koshinstudio.com/en/about/#operator) (web engineer and app engineer) · published 2026-10-16
A buying guide / October 2026

  There are many ways to protect Pokémon cards: sleeves, loaders, deck boxes, binders. This guide lists what to check before you buy, so that what you order actually fits.

  One thing first: this is not a hands-on comparison. I could not find an official size table from the manufacturers, so the numbers are the “commonly stated” ones from shop pages and explainer articles. I separate what I could confirm from what I could not, and I do not recommend a specific product.

## The short version: three things to check

    Check | How

    Card size | Pokémon cards are “standard size”, commonly stated as about 63 × 88mm. Sleeves made for “small size” cards (about 59 × 86mm, for example Yu-Gi-Oh!) may not fit.

    Sleeve size | Choose sleeves labeled for standard-size cards. Outer size is often listed as around 66 × 91mm. Read the product page’s “compatible size.”

    Loader “pt” | A thickness grade. A bigger number takes a thicker card. 35pt is the usual rule of thumb for an ordinary card.

## Sizes: standard and small

- Standard: Pokémon, Magic: The Gathering and others. Commonly about 63 × 88mm.

- Small: Yu-Gi-Oh!, Duel Masters, Weiß Schwarz and others. Commonly about 59 × 86mm.

  A standard card does not fit in a sleeve made for small cards. A small card in a standard sleeve is loose. Look for “for Pokémon cards” or “standard size” in the product name first.

  Several explainer articles agreed on these numbers, but I could not confirm them on an official Pokémon Card Game page.

## Sleeves: choose by use

- For play: use the same sleeve for every card in the deck. Differences in back pattern or color can show which cards are which (tournament rules differ, so check the rules of the event you enter).

- For storage: sleeves protect the surface. Some people double-sleeve valuable cards (inner sleeve plus outer sleeve).

- Count: bags of about 100 are common. A deck is 60 cards, so one bag is enough.

## Loaders: what “35pt” means

  “pt” is a unit of card thickness. 1pt is one thousandth of an inch (about 0.0254mm), so 35pt is about 0.89mm: roughly the thickness of one ordinary card.

- 35pt magnetic loaders: some shop pages list an outer size of 73 × 110 × 8mm, an inner size of 64 × 90mm and a compatible thickness of about 1mm.

- With the sleeve on: some loaders take a sleeved card, some do not. If you want to load a sleeved card, check that the product says so.

- Thicker cards: loaders of 55pt, 75pt, 100pt and more also exist, used for thick cards or sleeved cards.

  The sizes above come from shop pages, not from a manufacturer’s official figures. They differ by product.

## Other items: deck boxes, binders, box protectors

- Deck boxes: check how many sleeved cards it holds.

- Binders: check pockets per page (9-pocket and so on) and whether sleeved cards fit.

- Booster box protectors: check the box dimensions so it matches the sealed box you own.

## Buying checklist

- Decide what it is for (a deck you play, cards you store, a sealed box).

- Confirm standard size or small size.

- Read the product page’s compatible size and count.

- For loaders, check the pt and whether sleeved cards fit.

- Scan the reviews for “did not fit.”

## What I could not confirm

- The card size on an official Pokémon Card Game page

- Official inner-size tables for sleeves and loaders from manufacturers (I only saw shop-page figures)

- Whether a given product takes a sleeved card (I did not test)

- Quality or durability of any product (this is not a hands-on comparison)

  Checked on October 16, 2026. Products change; check the product page before you buy.

## Sources

- Torecamap: Pokémon card sleeve sizes (https://torecamap.co.jp/column/pokemoncard-sleeve-size/) (explainer, in Japanese)

- Torecamap: trading card sizes (https://torecamap.co.jp/column/tradingcard-size/) (explainer, in Japanese)

- 35pt loader sizes: several shop pages (not the manufacturer’s official figures)

  This is the English version of the original Japanese article (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/card-supplies-guide/).

  More in English

- All English pages (https://koshinstudio.com/en/)

  Languages: 日本語 (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/card-supplies-guide/)

# Draft Party

  日本語版 (https://koshinstudio.com/works/draft-party/)

  Pick any word you like. Tie with someone? Lottery!
A draft day for everyone, in your browser.

  Play now (https://koshinstudio.com/draft/)

  Free. Runs in your browser, no install or sign-up. Available in Japanese, English, Korean and Traditional Chinese.

    12teams at most
    2modes
    4languages

## What it is

  Name your team and pick words. In Round 1 everyone bids at the same time, hidden from the others, and all bids are revealed together. If teams chose the same word, they draw lots: the competing teams take turns picking one hidden paper, and when everyone has picked, all papers open at once. Only the winner gets the rights; the others re-bid with a different word.

  From Round 2, teams pick one at a time, and the order flips every round. At the end, the contract talks are announced — “signed” or “refused”. You can turn your result into an image and share it on X.

## Two modes

### Free-word mode

  Pick anything — a person, a food, any word, not just baseball. The host can set a theme, or everyone can vote for one.

### Scout mode

  Pick fictional rookies by their abilities, potential and records. The abilities are the scouts’ estimates and can differ from reality. Signed players grow over several years while every team plays every other team. You get yearly standings, head-to-head records against every team, titles such as batting champion and wins leader, Rookie of the Year and draft grades — revealed to everyone at the same time, so you can react together with stamps and chat. There is also a mode where the host registers the players.

## With friends, or with strangers

- Friends room: enter with a 6-character room code or a link. The host chooses the number of teams, rounds, time limit, mode and theme, and nothing starts until the host presses Start. Once your friends are in, the host can make the room public so random-match players can join. The host can also remove anyone who causes trouble.

- Random match: you are grouped with players using the same language. If there aren’t enough players, CPU teams join, so it starts without a wait.

  Every team gets an original emblem automatically (you can pick another), and you can use your own image in any room (inappropriate images are hidden after reports).

## How it is built

  The server (Cloudflare Workers with Durable Objects) runs all the progress and judging. Round 1 bids are not sent to anyone until the reveal, and the winning paper of a lottery is known only to the server until everyone has drawn. Even the host cannot peek at bids or rig a lottery. There is no login, and the sound effects and music are generated in the browser (no audio files).

  The players in Scout mode are fictional people generated at random each time. They have no connection to real players, teams or results, and this game has no connection to any professional league or team.

## What is stored

  For the sake of play inside a room, a device-generated number, your team name, what you pick, chat messages and the room settings are kept only for the life of that room, and are all deleted 10 minutes after the game ends. There is no ranking. Details are on the privacy page (https://koshinstudio.com/en/privacy/).

    Play now (https://koshinstudio.com/draft/)

# Koshin Studio

  A one-person studio. I build browser games and small apps, and write down what I measure.

  Free. No install, no sign-up.

## Play

- Sushi Stack (https://koshinstudio.com/play/sushitsumu/) — A falling-block puzzle: collide matching sushi toppings to grow them, all the way up to the golden sushi tub. Available in 14 languages, opens in your browser language. (About, English) (https://koshinstudio.com/en/works/sushitsumu/)

- Negaeri Shogi (https://koshinstudio.com/play/negaeri-shogi/) — A 6×6 board game. Pieces you sandwich defect to your side and get promoted, and chains flip many at once. Local, vs AI, and online with ratings. The game is in English and Japanese. (rules, English) (https://koshinstudio.com/en/works/negaeri-shogi/)

- Stop at 10 seconds (https://koshinstudio.com/play/stopwatch10/) — Count ten seconds in your head and stop. Best of three; the smaller the error, the stronger you are. No setup, no sign-up. The interface is in Japanese. (About, English) (https://koshinstudio.com/en/works/stopwatch10/)

- Anime Type Quiz (https://koshinstudio.com/app/shindananime/en/) — 12 questions, 6 axes: your anime type and the one anime that fits you right now. Free, nothing is sent anywhere. In English.

- “Checked” marks on articles that had never been read: the t.co relay page (https://koshinstudio.com/en/notes/tco-relay/)

- Notifications cannot be recalled: 19% of the last 72 hours’ notifications were wrong, and the gate worked after the fact (https://koshinstudio.com/en/notes/notify-gate/)

- Every deploy re-ran the daily jobs: 477 runs in 48 hours, 46.6% of that day’s Gemini cost (https://koshinstudio.com/en/notes/rerun-on-deploy/)

- Four times my own tools hurt me: a summary dropped conditions, one undefined stopped saving, a check locked out production, alerts that never cleared (https://koshinstudio.com/en/notes/self-inflicted/)

- Before widening concurrency slots: widening a 2-core server from 8 to 14, and the earlier conclusion that was half wrong (https://koshinstudio.com/en/notes/concurrency-slots/)

- “The same application page” does not mean “the same store”: 52 articles showed another store’s name (https://koshinstudio.com/en/notes/same-page-not-same-store/)

- Three mix-ups in splitting one article into products: a child treated as a parent, a shared link pointing to another store, a name owned by two products (https://koshinstudio.com/en/notes/split-mixups/)

- When first-come sales start, the site becomes a waiting-room page: a 15 KB notice slipped through an 8,000-byte gate (https://koshinstudio.com/en/notes/waiting-room/)

- 393 “work-name-only” products from an official list: the name field did not contain the product form (https://koshinstudio.com/en/notes/catalog-seed-393/)

- Comparing with other sites to count gaps: the first “23% coverage” was a measuring mistake and the truth was 49% (https://koshinstudio.com/en/notes/coverage-check/)

- I opened the links of displayed articles and compared them: about 60 mistakes, and three mistakes in my own first check (https://koshinstudio.com/en/notes/destination-check/)

- With no ads, 25 real-device checks were blocked: test ads in developer mode only, and no hard-coded prize names (https://koshinstudio.com/en/notes/test-ads/)

- I fixed a timeout three times and it did not stop: the culprit was a second process under the same lock (https://koshinstudio.com/en/notes/timeout-third-fix/)

- Looking up an ambiguous store name returns Shizuoka, the middle of Japan: I judged by Google’s own answer, not a list of chains (https://koshinstudio.com/en/notes/geocode-shizuoka/)

- Candidates were found, yet reading the answer failed every time: a URL cut at 200 tokens, and a search that returned 400 on hyphens (https://koshinstudio.com/en/notes/truncated-answer/)

- “One page = one case” was false: articles of a shop taking 6 products on one form were hidden just for sharing a link (https://koshinstudio.com/en/notes/one-page-many-cases/)

- “The server went down and I cannot recover it” was wrong: only inbound SSH had been blocked (https://koshinstudio.com/en/notes/misdiagnosis-down/)
